objectives.wording: Use a model to demonstrate the reference position, identify a requested plane, and describe the side, relative position and movement of a marked structure.
Annotate a bone section to distinguish its tissue and marrow components and summarize the composition of each.
Compare specimens from different bone types. Label their parts, explain their distinguishing features, and trace the routes of their vessels and nerves.
Identify a sesamoid bone on a model and explain how its position distinguishes it from nearby bones.
Use a sequence of developmental diagrams to explain the order of ossification, classify the labelled epiphyses and describe why each type matters.
Compare labelled cartilage specimens by structure and match each type to anatomical locations.
Classify joints on models, give an example of each requested subtype and demonstrate the movements allowed by selected joints.
Use a labelled limb diagram to explain the innervation of a selected joint and apply Hilton’s law to the structures shown.
Sort muscle examples by tissue structure and describe selected skeletal muscles by size, shape, location and action.
Label a muscle and its attachments, then distinguish a tendon from an aponeurosis using examples.
Compare the pull of a shunt and a spurt muscle on a joint model and explain the contribution of each to the movement shown.
Compare skin types at selected sites and locate a requested dermatome on a body diagram.
Identify skin layers and appendages on a section or model and relate one observed feature to a clinical example.
Compare proposed incision directions on a skin diagram and explain the anatomical principle and surgical implication of each.
Identify the contents of superficial fascia in a specimen or diagram and compare its modifications and fat distribution at selected sites.
Identify deep fascia modifications on a model, locate each example and explain its function.
Compare the routes and roles of blood vessels and lymphatic vessels on a labelled diagram.
Compare the gross features of an artery, vein and vascular sinus using labelled examples.
Compare elastic arteries, muscular arteries and arterioles by gross structure and explain the function of each class.
Use a microvascular diagram to explain how metarterioles, precapillary sphincters and arteriovenous connections affect flow.
Distinguish thrombosis, infarction and aneurysm using three labelled examples and explain which feature identifies each process.
Trace blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits and identify their connection points.
Trace a portal circuit on a diagram and explain which features make it a portal arrangement.
Identify examples of anastomoses, trace a potential collateral route and compare it with the supply of an end artery.
Label the main lymphatic components on a diagram and explain the role of each.
Identify features of a lymphatic capillary and trace lymph from tissue entry toward its return to the circulation.
Explain a simulated lymphatic obstruction using a drainage diagram and compare potential lymphatic and venous routes of tumour spread.
Draw an organizational map of the central, peripheral and autonomic components and place examples in their corresponding groups.
Identify the major cellular components of nervous tissue and match each to its function.
Label the parts of a neuron and classify examples by their processes, size and function.
Trace the parts of a typical spinal nerve on a labelled diagram and distinguish roots from branches.
Trace sensory and motor connections to a muscle on a diagram and explain the role of each route.
Use a simulated loss of muscle innervation to predict affected functions and explain the anatomical basis.
Compare labelled examples of synapses and classify them using the features shown.
Compare the location and organization of sympathetic and spinal ganglia on a labelled diagram.
Orient and side a sampled clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna or carpal bone where applicable. Demonstrate landmarks and articulations and explain a clinical correlation.
Show selected muscle footprints on a supplied upper-limb bone and name the attached muscles.
Locate the bones on an articulated hand, label parts of the metacarpals and phalanges, and explain what makes the pisiform distinctive.
Use a diagram to relate a fracture line and the direction of scaphoid blood supply to the risk of avascular necrosis.
Describe attachments, nerve supply and actions of pectoralis major and pectoralis minor; describe the clavipectoral fascia.
Map the breast's position, extent and deep relations. Connect microscopic features to gross structure and trace vascular and lymphatic routes to explain a clinical finding.
Draw a timeline of breast development and age-related changes and use it to account for selected congenital variants.
Orient a specimen or model and demonstrate the walls, apex, base and major contents.
Trace the axillary artery on a model, marking its limits, parts, relations and branches, then show the tributaries entering the axillary vein.
Label the axillary node groups on a regional diagram and match each to its principal drainage territory.
Trace drainage from the affected site in a vignette to the appropriate axillary groups and explain the pattern of nodal enlargement.
Trace roots to terminal branches on a specimen or model, demonstrate key relations and terminal courses, and map branch territories.
Compare a standard plexus diagram with a variant and explain which contributions or connections differ.
Use paired Erb and Klumpke vignettes to explain the characteristic findings from the affected plexus components.
Locate each muscle and demonstrate attachment sites, then relate position and innervation to action.
Trace a collateral route through the scapular arterial network and mark the triangle of auscultation on a separate surface sketch.
Identify the deltoid and individual cuff muscles on a specimen or model, pair each with its innervation and relate a selected injury to the structures involved.
On a specimen or model, describe and demonstrate serratus anterior attachments and actions, and explain relevant clinical anatomy.

Classify the joint on a model and show its surfaces, capsule, synovium, ligaments and relations. Demonstrate movements and the muscles involved, then explain vascular supply, innervation and a clinical correlation.
Trace the axillary nerve on a deltoid-region diagram and explain why its course makes it vulnerable during intramuscular injection.
On an arm specimen, distinguish the muscle compartments and show where biceps and triceps lie and how their arrangement supports their actions.
Trace major nerves and vessels from their entry into the arm to their endpoints on a model, pointing out key relations and branches or tributaries.
Describe the anatomical basis of cubital venipuncture, including relevant superficial venous location and neighbouring structures in a labelled diagram.
Outline the fossa on a specimen, identify its limits and show the positions of its principal contents.
Trace connections between arterial branches above and below the elbow on a diagram.
Use the course of the radial nerve in the arm to explain the findings after prolonged external compression.
Explain wrist drop in a lesion vignette by linking the affected nerve or branch to loss of extensor function.
Identify the main anterior forearm muscle groups on a specimen, show representative attachments and connect each muscle to its innervation and action.
On a model, follow the principal nerves and vessels through the anterior forearm, showing their origins, endpoints, neighbours and branches or tributaries.
Demonstrate the main posterior forearm muscle groups on a specimen, identifying their attachments and relating innervation to action.
Trace major nerves and vessels of the posterior forearm on a model, showing their origins, endpoints, key relations and branches or tributaries.
Identify the tendon compartments under the extensor retinaculum and show the boundaries and contents of the anatomical snuffbox.
Locate the flexor retinaculum on a wrist model and show its medial and lateral bony attachments.
Use a wrist cross-section to explain which nerve is compressed and how its course accounts for the characteristic findings.
Identify the intrinsic muscles on a hand model and match thumb movements to the muscles that produce them.
Demonstrate each major thumb movement and name the muscles responsible.
Follow the major nerves and blood vessels in a hand specimen and identify their principal branches.
On a model, distinguish the fibrous flexor sheaths, digital synovial sheaths and the radial and ulnar bursae, and show their relationships.
Use a cross-section to locate the major palmar fascial spaces and explain how their boundaries and communications affect the spread of infection.
Identify the extensor expansion on a digit model and show how the extensor tendon and intrinsic muscle contributions form it.
Use intrinsic and extrinsic muscle actions to explain the joint posture in a claw hand vignette.
Sketch the upper-limb fascial compartments and explain how fascia organizes their contents. Trace superficial and deep venous return and lymphatic drainage.
Label a dermatome map of the upper limb and identify the spinal root corresponding to a marked skin region.

On a model, locate the elbow, both radioulnar articulations, wrist and first carpometacarpal joint. Classify each and show its surfaces, capsule, synovial lining, stabilizers, relations and movements. Annotate its blood supply and innervation.
Describe the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular, carpometacarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints.
Identify the bones and joints visible on paired AP and lateral images of the shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm and hand.

Demonstrate the jugular notch, sternal angle, acromial angle, scapular spine and inferior scapular angle on a model, then estimate the vertebral levels of the medial end of the spine and inferior angle.

Mark the cephalic and basilic veins and demonstrate brachial and radial pulse palpation. Demonstrate a test for trapezius, pectoralis major, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi, deltoid, biceps and brachioradialis.
Draw a developmental sequence showing limb bud growth, patterning, rotation and digit separation in the upper limb.
Sequence limb-bud growth, digit formation and rotation, and relate rotation to the adult orientation of the lower limb.
Identify and orient a sampled hip bone, femur, tibia, fibula or tarsal. Determine its side where applicable, show its landmarks and articulations, and explain one clinical correlation.
Use a supplied lower-limb bone to identify each joint it forms and describe the corresponding articular surfaces.
Explain the significance of ossification at the distal femur and proximal tibia. Use the fibula to illustrate the exception to the usual relationship between epiphyseal ossification and fusion.
Identify each bone on an articulated foot model and show the muscle attachment sites on the individual bones.
Trace the major nerves and vessels on a specimen or model, demonstrating origins, endpoints, key relations and branches or tributaries.
Identify the major anterior thigh muscles on a specimen, demonstrate their attachments and relate each muscle to its innervation and actions.
Locate the canal on a model, demonstrate its boundaries and extent, and trace the structures that pass through it.
Identify the hamstrings on a specimen, demonstrate their attachments and explain how their innervation and joint crossings relate to their actions.
Trace the major nerves and vessels through the posterior thigh on a model. Show their origins, endpoints, relations and branches or tributaries.
Outline the triangle on a specimen and demonstrate its floor, roof and principal contents in relation to one another.
Explain the anatomical basis of psoas abscess.
Explain the anatomical basis of femoral hernia.
On a specimen, identify the principal gluteal muscles, show their attachment sites and relate each muscle to its innervation and actions.
Lift the gluteus maximus on a model or use a prepared specimen to locate the deep structures. Trace the sciatic nerve and explain its vulnerability to misplaced injections.
Use a single-leg stance diagram to explain the role of the hip abductors in pelvic stability and predict which side of the pelvis drops when they fail.
Demonstrate the boundaries, roof and floor on a specimen. Show the relative depth and position of its contents and use those relations to explain a clinical finding.
Classify the joint on a model and show its surfaces, capsule, synovium, ligaments, bursae and relations. Demonstrate movements and the muscles involved, and map its vascular supply and innervation.
Use a diagram of the femoral head blood supply and a fracture location to explain the anatomical basis of impaired healing and osteonecrosis.
Explain the anatomical basis of hip dislocation and of hip replacement.
Locate the principal anterior compartment muscles on a specimen, demonstrate their attachments and relate their innervation to ankle and toe movements.
Trace the major nerves and vessels in the anterior compartment, showing their origins, endpoints, key relations and branches or tributaries.
Distinguish superficial and deep posterior leg muscles on a specimen, demonstrate their attachments and connect each muscle to its innervation and action.
Trace major nerves and vessels through the back of the leg, showing their origins, endpoints, relations and branches or tributaries.
Relate loss of ankle dorsiflexion to weak muscles in a lesion vignette and explain how associated findings help localize the lesion.

Classify the joint on a model and demonstrate its surfaces, capsule, synovium, ligaments, bursae and surrounding relations. Show the movements and muscles involved, and trace its innervation and periarticular arterial network.
Use a movement sequence to explain rotation during terminal extension and how the knee returns to a position that permits flexion.
Use injury vignettes to connect a force direction and the resulting instability or mechanical symptoms to the injured ligament or meniscus.
Explain the anatomical basis of osteoarthritis of the knee joint.
Explain how calf contraction and venous valves work together to move blood proximally during walking.
Trace force from the calf muscles to the calcaneus and explain how interrupting the tendon affects plantarflexion and push-off.
Locate the arches on a diagram and explain how bone shape, ligaments, fascia and muscles support load distribution during stance and gait.
Explain the anatomical basis of flatfoot and clubfoot.
Compare the relevant load-bearing structures in forefoot pain and plantar heel pain, using the metatarsal heads and proximal plantar fascia as landmarks.

Use an articulated model to distinguish the proximal and distal tibiofibular joints from the ankle. Show their surfaces, capsules, synovial linings where present, ligaments and nearby structures. Demonstrate motion and identify the muscles, nerves and vessels involved.
Sketch the articulations of the hindfoot and midfoot at these joints and explain how motion at them contributes to inversion and eversion.
Show the fascia lata and retinacula on a model. Trace superficial and deep venous and lymphatic pathways and mark lower-limb dermatomes on a separate map.
Explain the anatomical basis of enlarged inguinal lymph nodes.
Explain the anatomical basis of varicose veins.
Explain the anatomical basis of deep vein thrombosis.
Identify the bones and joint spaces on paired AP and lateral lower-limb radiographs and use visible landmarks to orient each image.

Locate pelvic, thigh, knee, leg and foot landmarks on a model or standardized subject. Include the specified pelvic vertebral levels, bony prominences around the knee and ankle, and medial and lateral foot landmarks.
Demonstrate femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, anterior tibial and dorsalis pedis palpation sites in simulation, using a palpable model or landmarks where needed.

Mark the femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, the midinguinal point and saphenous opening. Add the femoral, sciatic, tibial, common fibular and deep fibular nerves and both saphenous veins on separate overlays.
